issues.quote: Churn means no spend in the 60 days after the snapshot. It reports: 'Churn by snapshot month: 11, 12, 11, 12, 6 and 2 percent.'
issues.explanation: The question pairs the course's inactivity definition ('no spend in the 60 days after the snapshot') and 'one snapshot per month' with a pattern ('6 and 2 percent') and explanation ('advertisers who will still leave are sitting in the stayed column') that only hold for point-in-time events like account cancellations. Under 'no spend at all in the 60 days after the snapshot', any advertiser who has already spent since the snapshot has positive 60-day spend and can never become a churner for that snapshot even if they stop later. Meanwhile, querying spend == 0 on an unclosed window makes recent churn spike upward (every true 60-day churner has zero spend so far, plus temporary pausers have zero spend so far), and defaulting unclosed monthly snapshots to stayed would produce 0% for an entire unclosed snapshot date, not 6% and 2%.
issues.evidence: facts.json -> data.outcome_columns.churned_next_60d = 'no spend at all in the 60 days after the snapshot'; monotonicity of cumulative spend: spend_60d == 0 implies spend_td == 0 for all t < 60.
issues.fix: Either change the rule in the stem to a point-in-time event ('Churn means cancelling an account within 60 days of the snapshot'), or keep 'no spend in the 60 days after the snapshot' and flip the error direction: 'Churn by snapshot month: 11, 12, 11, 12, 18 and 35 percent. Churn is surging.' with keyed answer 'The newest snapshots' 60 days are not over, so temporary pausers with no spend yet count as churned'.

issues.quote: An advertiser whose snapshot was 20 days ago has not survived 60 days. They have survived 20. Label them as stayed, and you have filed some future churners under loyal.
issues.explanation: This contradicts the 60-day zero-spend definition just taught in the predict question and seg1 ('no spend at all in the 60 days after a snapshot date'). Under that definition, an advertiser who spent during the first 20 days already has spend inside the 60-day window and cannot become a churner for that snapshot even if they stop on day 21. Conversely, an advertiser with zero spend in those 20 days has not 'survived 20'—they are undecided between a temporary pause and a 60-day churn (and naive spend == 0 queries file pausers under churned, while only a default-to-stayed rule files already-silent accounts under stayed).
issues.evidence: predict & seg1 narration ('no spend at all in the 60 days after a snapshot date... Under that definition the three-week pauser stayed: they spent again inside the window') vs seg3 narration.
issues.fix: Replace with wording consistent with the 60-day zero-spend rule: 'An advertiser with no spend in the 20 days since their snapshot is still undecided: they might be gone for good, or on a three-week pause. Count zero spend so far as churned and pausers look like churners; default open windows to stayed and real churners hide under loyal.' (Or explicitly specify 'If churn means cancelling within 60 days...' for the survival example.)

issues.quote: Why can you not label an advertiser as retained when their snapshot was three weeks ago? ... some of them will still churn.
issues.explanation: In the context of the lesson's churn rule ('no spend at all in the 60 days after a snapshot'), an advertiser who has spent during the first three weeks is already retained for that 60-day window and cannot 'still churn' for that snapshot. What is unknown at three weeks is whether advertisers with zero spend so far will return before day 60, which also makes the whole three-week-old cohort unusable because stayers become confirmed early while churners can only be confirmed at day 60.
issues.evidence: facts.json -> data.outcome_columns.churned_next_60d = 'no spend at all in the 60 days after the snapshot'; seg1 narration.
issues.fix: Change the drill question and answer to match the 60-day zero-spend rule: Q: 'Churn means no spend in the sixty days after a snapshot. Why can you not include a snapshot from three weeks ago in your training table?' A: 'Because its sixty-day outcome window has not closed. Advertisers with no spend so far might be churners or merely on a three-week pause, and keeping only the ones who already spent would drop every future churner.'

verdict: All figures cited from the simulated dataset (monthly churn rates, tracking rates, advertiser counts, and CPA goal hit rates) match facts.json accurately, but seg3, quiz 1-3-q1, and drill 2 conflate 'no spend at all in 60 days' with 'cancels within 60 days', reversing what happens when an outcome window has not yet closed.
